title: About
description: Headquartered in West Chester, Ohio, with chapters in Kentucky, Florida, and Mississippi. The story and mission of W.I.S.E.C.E.O., a 501(c)(3) nonprofit dismantling barriers to technology, education, and economic opportunity.
text: Our Story Excellence is not a privilege. It's a right. W.I.S.E.C.E.O. is a 501(c)(3) nonprofit dedicated to dismantling systemic barriers that prevent underserved communities from accessing technology, education, and economic opportunity. We serve first-generation learners, immigrants, refugees, and low-income youth and adults — communities historically underrepresented in technology and the workforce. Founded and led by educators with more than 30 years in the public school system, we've reached over 25,000 students across our chapters to date. Through coding education, digital literacy, career pathway development, and entrepreneurship support, we equip individuals with the critical skills needed to succeed in today's innovation economy — generating measurable, lasting economic impact. Digital Equity Workforce Readiness Innovation Economy Job Creation Economic Resilience Underserved Communities 🌍 Worldwide Reach Programs serving communities across the globe, with a focus on under-resourced regions. 💡 Tech & Innovation Bridging the digital divide with coding, creativity, and technology education. 📊 Economic Impact Measurable job creation, private investment, and long-term community prosperity. ✊ Equity First Every program designed to remove barriers and create genuine access to opportunity. Where We Serve Rooted in Ohio. Growing across the country. W.I.S.E.C.E.O. is headquartered in West Chester, Ohio, and serves learners, families, and educators through community chapters in Kentucky, Florida, and Mississippi. Our impact reaches learners from 35 nations — and new communities join every year. Students we teach and mentor take part in programs led by respected national, regional and civic organizations. 💻 Amazon Future Engineer Students participate in Amazon’s childhood-to-career computer science and STEM program, connecting classroom learning with real engineers and technology careers. Amazon Future Engineer → ☁️ AWS Community Engagement Amazon Web Services community and STEM programs that bring technology education, volunteers and career exposure to local learners. AWS Community Engagement → 🏅 TechOlympics Students have competed in TechOlympics, the nation’s largest student-run technology conference, held in Greater Cincinnati. TechOlympics → 💼 DC Department of Employment Services Partnered to connect program youth with structured career pathways, technical training and hands-on professional apprenticeships. DC DOES → 🏛️ DC Council & Civic Leadership Collaborated directly with Councilmember offices through the Jack and Jill of America On the Hill Legislative Summit to advocate for youth development policy and expand our collaborative network. Council of the District of Columbia → Meet Our Founder Tiffany Davidson, M.Ed., M.Ed. Tiffany Davidson is an educator, literacy advocate, and language-acquisition specialist who founded W.I.S.E.C.E.O. to open the doors that education opened for her. She holds two master’s degrees — in Literacy and Language Acquisition from the University of Cincinnati, and in Curriculum & Instruction from the University of Southern Mississippi — and a B.S. in English from the University of Southern Mississippi, along with certifications in TESOL and English Language Arts, and training in gifted and Section 504 services and administrative leadership. Her classroom work spans high schools in Ohio, Florida, and Mississippi. As ESL department chair and STEAM Club advisor at Western Hills High School in Cincinnati, she taught 150 multilingual students and mentored student STEM projects in partnership with TechOlympics and Amazon engineers. Before returning to the classroom, she spent more than a decade in business development, marketing, and financial services, experience she now brings to financial literacy education. Her work centers on the learners schools too often overlook: English language learners, immigrant and refugee families, first-generation students, and students with IEPs. As a literacy advocate, she helps teachers make every lesson accessible through research-based approaches such as SIOP and differentiated instruction, and she helps families understand and use their rights so their children get the support they deserve. At W.I.S.E.C.E.O., that experience powers our belief that literacy is the first job skill — and the foundation of economic mobility. title: Accessibility
description: How W.I.S.E.C.E.O. makes its website usable for every family: language options, high contrast, keyboard access, and how to report a barrier.
text: Accessibility A website for every family. Last updated: October 2026 W.I.S.E.C.E.O. serves multilingual learners, families, and communities who have too often been left out. We want everyone to be able to read, navigate, and act on the information on this website, whatever language they speak and however they use the web. What we have built in Language selector: choose a language from the menu at the top of any page. Pages are translated automatically by Google Translate, so wording may not be perfect. For anything important, such as program applications, contact us and we will help. High-contrast mode: turn on the High contrast switch at the top of any page. Your choice is remembered on this device. If your device is set to prefer more contrast, we turn it on for you. Keyboard access: every menu, button, and form can be used with a keyboard. Use the “Skip to main content” link, press / to search, and press Esc to close menus. Screen readers: we use page landmarks, headings, labels, and text alternatives for images. Mobile friendly: the site adapts to phones and tablets and respects reduced-motion settings. Our goal We aim to meet the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2 at Level AA. This is ongoing work, and some content, including donation and form tools provided by other companies, may not yet fully meet that standard. Tell us about a barrier If something on this site is hard to use, or you need information in another format or language, please contact us or email admin@wiseceo.org . Tell us the page and what happened, and we will respond as quickly as we can.

title: Your Child's IEP, Explained: A Family Guide to the Meeting Table
description: What an IEP is, what your rights are, and the questions to bring — especially if your family speaks a language other than English at home
text: News & Resources · October 2026 Your Child's IEP, Explained: A Family Guide to the Meeting Table What an IEP is, what your rights are, and the questions to bring — especially if your family speaks a language other than English at home Family Advocacy IEP & Special Education Education Access Every fall, families across Ohio sit down at a table with teachers, specialists and administrators to talk about one thing: how their child is going to learn this year. If you have ever walked out of an IEP meeting feeling rushed, confused or unheard, you are not alone — and you are not powerless. As an educator and literacy advocate, I have sat on every side of that table. This guide is the one I wish every family had before their first meeting. What is an IEP? An Individualized Education Program (IEP) is a written plan for a student who qualifies for special education under the federal law known as IDEA (the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act). It describes: How your child is doing right now (their "present levels") Measurable goals for the year The services, supports and accommodations the school will provide How progress will be measured and reported to you An IEP is not a label. It is a promise — in writing — about what your child will receive. Five rights every family should know You are a member of the IEP team. Not a guest. Your knowledge of your child counts as data. You can request an evaluation in writing. If you think your child needs help, put the request in an email or letter and keep a copy. You can ask for a meeting at any time. The IEP must be reviewed at least once a year, but you do not have to wait for the annual meeting if something is not working. You have the right to understand what is happening. If your family's primary language is not English, the school must take steps to make sure you understand the meeting — including arranging an interpreter. Ask for one ahead of time. You can take time before you sign. It is okay to say, "I'd like to take this home and review it." For families of English learners: A student can receive English language services and special education services at the same time. Learning English is not a disability — but a student who is learning English can also have a disability. If you are told your child has to "wait until their English improves" before being evaluated, ask the team to explain that decision in writing. Questions to bring to the table What do my child's assessment results actually show, in plain language? Which goal matters most this year, and how will we know it is working? How often will my child receive each service, and who provides it? What accommodations will my child have in class and on tests? How and how often will I get progress updates? What can we do at home to support the goals? Literacy belongs in the IEP conversation Reading touches every subject — science labs, word problems, history, even the instructions on a test. If your child is struggling with reading, ask the team directly: What does my child's reading data show, what is the specific skill gap, and what research-based intervention will close it? Vague answers like "we'll keep an eye on it" are a signal to ask for more detail. A simple routine before every meeting Ask for draft documents a few days early. Write down your top three concerns and your child's top three strengths. Bring a support person — a relative, friend or advocate. Take notes, and ask for a copy of everything you sign. Ohio resources Ohio families can find the state's parent guide to special education, Whose IDEA Is This? , through the Ohio Department of Education and Workforce, and free training and support through the Ohio Coalition for the Education of Children with Disabilities (OCECD), Ohio's federally funded parent center. Education is the first door to economic opportunity. When families know their rights, kids get the support they need — and that changes what is possible for the whole family. With you at the table, Tiffany Davidson, M.Ed., M.Ed. W.I.S.E.C.E.O. — Creating Equity & Opportunity This newsletter shares general educational information, not legal advice. For questions about a specific situation, contact your school district or a qualified advocate. Get free guides in your inbox. title: Reading Is the First Job Skill: Why Literacy Is Workforce Development
description: Every career pathway — healthcare, manufacturing, the trades, technology — starts with reading. Here's how families can build it at home, at any age.
text: News & Resources · October 2026 Reading Is the First Job Skill: Why Literacy Is Workforce Development Every career pathway — healthcare, manufacturing, the trades, technology — starts with reading. Here's how families can build it at home, at any age. Literacy Workforce Development Family Advocacy When people talk about workforce development, they usually picture welding booths, hospital simulation labs or coding bootcamps. Those matter. But long before anyone earns a credential, there is a skill underneath every single one of them: reading. A nursing student reads medication orders. An apprentice electrician reads code requirements and wiring diagrams. A lab technician reads safety data sheets. A small-business owner reads contracts, loan terms and tax forms. Literacy is not separate from economic mobility — it is the foundation of it. What "literacy" really means today Literacy is more than sounding out words. It includes: Decoding and fluency — reading words accurately and smoothly Vocabulary — knowing what words mean, including the technical words of a field Comprehension — understanding, remembering and questioning what you read Writing — explaining your thinking clearly Digital literacy — finding, judging and using information online Five habits families can start this week Read together for 15 minutes a day. Any book, any language. Reading in your home language builds the same thinking skills — and those skills transfer to English. Talk about what you read. Ask, "What do you think will happen next?" or "Why did they do that?" Conversation builds comprehension. Collect "big words." When your child meets a new word, write it on a sticky note and use it at dinner. Vocabulary grows through use. Read the real world. Recipes, bus schedules, job postings, instructions for a new phone. Show kids that reading gets things done. Get a library card. Ohio's public libraries offer free books, e-books, homework help and computer access. For teens and young adults: Pick one career you are curious about and read three things from that field this month — a job posting, an article and a training program description. Circle every word you don't know. That list is your career vocabulary, and learning it puts you ahead. When to ask for help If your child avoids reading, guesses at words, reads slowly and tiredly, or understands much more when you read to them than when they read alone, those are signals worth sharing with their teacher. Ask what the school's reading assessments show and what support is available. Early help works — and it is never too late to start. Where W.I.S.E.C.E.O. fits in Our programs connect literacy to opportunity: digital literacy and coding, education access for first-generation students and English learners, and workforce pathways into Ohio's growth industries. In future issues, we'll share free resources, family guides and stories from learners building their futures one page at a time. Keep reading — together, Tiffany Davidson, M.Ed., M.Ed. title: Six SIOP Moves Every Teacher Can Use Tomorrow With English Learners
description: Practical, research-based strategies from a literacy advocate and ESL educator — no new curriculum required
text: News & Resources · October 2026 Six SIOP Moves Every Teacher Can Use Tomorrow With English Learners Practical, research-based strategies from a literacy advocate and ESL educator — no new curriculum required Literacy English Learners Teacher Strategies English learners are one of the fastest-growing groups of students in Ohio classrooms — and one of the most underserved. The good news: the strategies that help English learners succeed make lessons clearer for every student. The SIOP Model (Sheltered Instruction Observation Protocol) is a research-based framework for teaching content and academic language at the same time. It has eight components: Lesson Preparation, Building Background, Comprehensible Input, Strategies, Interaction, Practice & Application, Lesson Delivery, and Review & Assessment. You don't need to master all eight at once. Start with these six moves. 1. Post a language objective next to your content objective Content objective: "Students will explain how the water cycle works." Language objective: "Students will use sequence words — first, next, then, finally — to describe the water cycle orally and in writing." When students know what language they're practicing, they use it on purpose. 2. Pre-teach five words, not twenty-five Choose the few words students truly need to access the lesson. Show a picture, act it out, connect it to a home-language word when you can, and keep the words visible on a word wall all week. 3. Give sentence frames for academic talk "I agree with ___ because ___." "The evidence that shows ___ is ___." "One difference between ___ and ___ is ___." Frames lower the risk of speaking and raise the level of the conversation. 4. Make input comprehensible Slow down, pause, and use visuals, gestures, models and real objects. Write key directions on the board as well as saying them, and model the task before students try it. 5. Structure interaction every 10 minutes Turn-and-talk, Think-Pair-Share, numbered heads — short, structured talk gives every learner practice using new language, not just the confident few. 6. Check understanding without asking "Does everyone get it?" Use thumbs up/sideways/down, whiteboards, quick exit tickets or "show me with your fingers." Then reteach right away for students who need it. Coach's tip: Pick one move this week and use it in every lesson. Ask a colleague to watch for it. Small, consistent changes beat big one-time overhauls. Remember the families A student's home language is an asset, not an obstacle. Encourage families to read, talk and tell stories at home in the language they know best — strong first-language skills support English literacy. Teaching with you, Tiffany Davidson, M.Ed., M.Ed. title: Taxing the Unbanked: Why Ohio Should Protect Check-Cashing and Payday Borrowers
description: A proposed revenue idea, more than a decade of Ohio reform, and the protections every borrower can use today
text: News & Resources · October 2026 Taxing the Unbanked: Why Ohio Should Protect Check-Cashing and Payday Borrowers A proposed revenue idea, more than a decade of Ohio reform, and the protections every borrower can use today Policy Financial Capability Ohio By Tiffany Davidson, Founder and CEO, Worldwide Institute for Success & Excellence (W.I.S.E.C.E.O.) States and school districts are always looking for new revenue, and some ideas sound easy until you ask who would pay. One proposal that comes up in school finance discussions is a tax on people who cash checks or borrow at storefront lenders, charged on the size of the check or the amount borrowed. I recently evaluated that idea against the standard tests for a revenue source, and the answer was clear. It would raise little money, and it would collect that money from the households with the least. This article has two parts. The first explains why this tax works against Ohio's own policy. The second is a practical guide for anyone using these lenders today. Part 1: Why this tax falls on the wrong people A small base made up of struggling households In 2023, about 4.2 percent of U.S. households had no bank account, and another 14.2 percent had an account but still used services such as check cashing or payday loans (FDIC, 2024). These households are concentrated at lower incomes. A tax built on their transactions takes a larger share of income from families who can least afford it, which makes it regressive. It is also unequal for people in the same situation. Two workers cashing the same $800 paycheck would pay different amounts depending only on whether one of them has a bank account. And because the base is narrow and shrinking as more people move to bank accounts and payment apps, the revenue would be small and unpredictable. Ohio has spent years lowering these costs Ohio lawmakers and voters have worked for more than a decade to protect the same borrowers this tax would target: 1996: H.B. 313 let check-cashing businesses make small loans, with annual rates that could reach 390 percent or more (Schiff, 2022). 2008: H.B. 545, the Short-Term Loan Act, limited these loans to $500 with a 28 percent annual rate, and voters upheld it at referendum. Lenders then moved to other lending laws and credit services brokers, where fees were unregulated, and no lender licensed under the new law for the next ten years (Schiff, 2022). 2014: The Ohio Supreme Court ruled unanimously that payday-style loans made under the Mortgage Loan Act were allowed, which kept those workarounds open (Toledo Blade, 2014). 2018: The Ohio Fairness in Lending Act, H.B. 123, required payday-type lenders to license under the Short-Term Loan Law and capped total interest and fees at 60 percent of the amount borrowed. Supporters estimated Ohio borrowers would save more than $75 million a year (Bourke, 2018). A new tax on these customers would add back part of the cost the state has worked to remove. It could also push borrowers toward unlicensed online lenders, which hurts families and shrinks the revenue at the same time. Ohio can find school revenue in broad-based sources with low rates that do not single out families already paying the most for basic financial services. Part 2: Know your rights and your options If you or someone in your family is using a payday or short-term lender in Ohio, these protections and resources can help. The rules for licensed short-term loans in Ohio Under H.B. 123, loans from licensed short-term lenders must follow these limits (Ohio Legislative Service Commission, n.d.; Legal Aid of Western Ohio, 2020): Loan size: No more than $1,000, and no more than $2,500 owed to one lender at a time. Interest: No more than 28 percent per year. Monthly fee: No more than 10 percent of the loan or $30, whichever is less. Total cost: All fees and charges together cannot exceed 60 percent of the amount you originally borrowed. Time to repay: At least 91 days, unless your monthly payment is no more than 6 percent of your gross monthly income or 7 percent of your net monthly income. The longest term allowed is one year. Payments: Equal installments that steadily reduce what you owe. If a lender is breaking the rules Add up everything you have paid in interest and fees. If the total is more than 60 percent of what you borrowed, or the lender is not licensed, you can file a complaint with the Ohio Division of Financial Institutions, Office of Consumer Affairs, at (866) 278-0003. You can also get free legal help. Legal Aid of Western Ohio can be reached at 1-877-894-4599, and OhioLegalHelp.org can connect you with the legal aid office in your county. Safer ways to borrow Many federal credit unions offer Payday Alternative Loans (PALs). They cap interest at 28 percent, limit the application fee to $20, and do not allow rollovers (Experian, n.d.). PAL I: $200 to $1,000, repaid over 1 to 6 months, for members who have belonged to the credit union for at least one month. PAL II: Up to $2,000, repaid over 1 to 12 months, with no waiting period after you join. Ask your local credit union whether it offers PALs or a small installment loan that can pay off a payday balance. Help with bills and debt Call 2-1-1. Ohio's 2-1-1 lines connect you with local help, including your county's Community Action Agency, which may offer emergency assistance with bills and, in some counties, matched savings programs. Talk with a nonprofit credit counselor. Apprisen, based in Gahanna, Ohio, offers debt management programs that combine your payments into one plan. Three steps to take this week Gather your loan papers and total what you have paid in interest and fees so far. Call your credit union about a PAL or another small installment loan. Dial 2-1-1 and ask for your Community Action Agency or a nonprofit credit counselor. Why this matters to W.I.S.E.C.E.O. description: W.I.S.E.C.E.O. is a 501(c)(3) nonprofit creating equity and opportunity through digital literacy, workforce development, and economic mobility for underserved communities.

title: Literacy & Language Access
description: W.I.S.E.C.E.O. brings research-based literacy and language instruction to English learners, first-generation students, families, and educators — the foundation of economic mobility.
text: Literacy & Language Access Literacy is the first door to opportunity. Every career pathway — healthcare, advanced manufacturing, the skilled trades, technology — begins with the ability to read, write, and communicate with confidence. For English language learners, immigrant and refugee families, first-generation students, and students with disabilities, that foundation is too often left to chance. W.I.S.E.C.E.O.’s literacy and language work brings research-based reading and language instruction to the learners and families who need it most, and equips the educators who serve them. It is the heart of our Education Access & Equity program — and the foundation under every workforce pathway we build. Family Literacy English Learners SIOP IEP & 504 Navigation Educator Learning 📖 Read together Fifteen minutes a day, in any language, builds the thinking skills that transfer to English. 🗣️ Talk to learn Structured conversation turns new words into real academic language. 🧩 Plan for every learner Language objectives, visuals, and sentence frames make lessons accessible to all. 🏛️ Know your rights Families who understand IEPs and 504 plans get the support their children deserve. What We Do How we build literacy. 👨‍👩‍👧 Family Literacy Practical guides and gatherings that help parents and caregivers build reading habits at home — in English or their home language — and connect reading to school and career goals. Families 🌐 English Learner Support SIOP-informed strategies, vocabulary and academic-language development, and resources for multilingual learners and newcomer students at every age. English Learners 🤝 Family Advocacy & IEP Navigation Plain-language workshops and guides that help families understand special education, IEPs, and 504 plans — including families who speak a language other than English. Families 🧑‍🏫 Educator Learning Practical strategies for teachers and paraprofessionals — differentiation, SIOP, and literacy across the content areas — so every classroom works for every learner. Educators 💼 Career & Digital Literacy Reading for the workforce: technical vocabulary, job applications, workplace communication, and the digital skills today’s employers expect. Youth & Adults 📰 Free Resources Family guides, teacher strategies, and policy updates delivered free through our newsletter. Read the newsletter → Led by a Literacy Specialist “ When a child learns to read — and a family learns to advocate — the whole family’s future changes. Literacy is the first job skill. Tiffany Davidson, M.Ed. — Founder, W.I.S.E.C.E.O. Our literacy work is led by an educator with master’s degrees in Literacy & Language Acquisition and Curriculum & Instruction , TESOL certification, and decades of experience in public education. Meet our founder → Bring literacy to your school or community. Get in Touch Support This Work

Training and resources that lead to real jobs, from hospitals and labs to job sites and farms. 🩺 Healthcare ⚗️ Manufacturing & Chemistry 🔧 Skilled Trades & Construction 🌾 Food & Agriculture Spotlight: Skilled Trades Get paid to learn a skilled trade, with no tuition bill and no college debt. Registered apprenticeships let you earn a paycheck while you train for in-demand trades like electrical, welding, and advanced manufacturing. Apprenticeship.gov lists openings you can search by trade and location. Who qualifies: Career pivoters and job seekers who want hands-on work, plus local employers who want to train their own talent. Most programs accept ages 18+ (some 16+) with a diploma or GED. The path: Search Apprenticeship.gov for your trade and area, contact the program or employer, and apply. Once accepted, you work and train at the same time. Most programs last 1 to 5 years, and many skilled trades take about 4. The outcome: A paid position from day one, plus a nationally recognized credential when you finish. Your pay rises as your skills grow. Starting wages vary by trade and employer. Your action step today: Go to Apprenticeship.gov , select “Find Apprenticeships,” and search your zip code for one electrical, welding, or manufacturing program. Save the contact info and send your first inquiry. Resources Resources worth your time. Workforce Micro-Credentials TechCred Ohio's TechCred program reimburses employers up to $1,000 per credential (up to $30,000 per application) when workers complete approved short-term tech certifications. Ask your employer to apply. Search apprenticeship openings → Digital Equity & Device Access Digital Inclusion Programs State programs are expanding low-cost high-speed internet and hardware in urban and underserved neighborhoods. Explore BroadbandOhio → Integrated English & Career Training Learn English While You Train Ohio's Aspire program pairs English classes (ESOL) with career training, so adult learners can build workplace English while working toward an industry credential. Look for free classes at community colleges, libraries, or vocational centers in your county. Find an Aspire provider → Foreign Credential Recognition Unlock Your International Degree Many skilled immigrants with degrees earned abroad work below their training. Nonprofits like Upwardly Global offer career coaching and guidance on credential review, U.S.-style resumes, and state licensing for work-authorized immigrants, refugees, and asylees. Upwardly Global job seeker resources → Immigrant Entrepreneurship Building Local Enterprise Community Development Financial Institutions (CDFIs) and the Small Business Administration offer micro-loans, mentorship, and technical assistance for small business owners, including immigrant and refugee founders who may lack U.S. credit history. title: Privacy Policy
description: How W.I.S.E.C.E.O. collects, uses, and protects your information.
text: Privacy Policy Your privacy matters. Last updated: October 2026 W.I.S.E.C.E.O. (Worldwide Institute for Success & Excellence) is a 501(c)(3) nonprofit organization based in West Chester, Ohio (EIN 41-3404888). Our mailing address is 7240 Towne Centre Blvd, Suite 78, West Chester, OH 45069. This policy explains what information we collect through www.wiseceo.org, how we use it, and the choices you have. Information we collect Contact form: your name, email address, area of interest, and message. Messages are delivered to us by email through our form service, Web3Forms, and saved in our secure Airtable database so we can follow up. We also note which language you were viewing the site in, so we can reply in that language when possible. Donations: donations are processed securely by Donorbox and its payment processors. We receive your name, email, donation amount, and any information you choose to share. We never see or store your full card or bank details. Newsletter: if you sign up, your email address is saved in our Airtable database and stored by our newsletter provider, beehiiv, which sends the newsletter. Translation: if you choose a language other than English from the language menu, the page is translated by Google Translate. Google receives the page text and standard technical data such as your IP address, and a cookie named googtrans remembers your language choice. If you keep the site in English, no Google service is loaded. See Google’s Privacy Policy . Videos: our videos are hosted on YouTube. An embedded video loads from YouTube (in privacy-enhanced mode) only when you press play; YouTube and Google may then receive standard technical data and set cookies under Google’s Privacy Policy . Display settings: if you turn on high-contrast mode, that choice is saved only in your own browser. It is never sent to us. Basic technical data: our hosting provider, Vercel, may log standard information such as IP address, browser type, and pages visited to keep the site secure and working. How we use your information To respond to your questions and requests To process donations and send tax receipts To send our newsletter and program updates if you subscribe To keep our website secure and improve it What we don’t do We do not sell, rent, or trade your personal information. We do not show advertising on this website. We share information only with the service providers listed above, to do the work you asked for, or when required by law. Your choices Unsubscribe from our newsletter at any time using the link in any email. Ask us to access, correct, or delete the personal information we hold about you by contacting us. Children’s privacy This website is intended for adults — families, educators, donors, and partners. We do not knowingly collect personal information online from children under 13. If you believe a child has sent us personal information, please contact us and we will delete it. Security Our website uses HTTPS encryption, and we rely on reputable providers to protect the information you share with us. No method of transmission over the internet is 100% secure, but we take reasonable steps to protect your data. Changes to this policy We may update this policy from time to time. The date at the top of this page shows when it was last revised. Contact us Questions about this policy? Contact us or write to us at 7240 Towne Centre Blvd, Suite 78, West Chester, OH 45069.
